entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen10101" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Thanksgiving Song of One Who Has Escaped from Death</title> <div sID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> We have here another anonymous Psalm closing with <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi>. It is not a supplicatory song with a hopeful prospect before it like Ps 115, but a thanksgiving song with a fresh recollection of some deadly peril that has just been got the better of; and is not, like Ps 115, from the mouth of the church, but from the lips of an individual who distinguishes himself from the church. It is an individual that has been delivered who here praises the loving-kindness he has experienced in the language of the tenderest affection. The lxx has divided this deeply fervent song into two parts, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.1-Ps.116.9">Psa 116:1-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10-Ps.116.19">Psa 116:10-19</reference>, and made two Hallelujah-Psalms out of it; whereas it unites <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1-Ps.114.8">Psa 114:1-8</reference> and Ps 115 into one. The four sections or strophes, the beginnings of which correspond to one another (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.1">Psa 116:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.5">Psa 116:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.116.15">Psa 116:15</reference>), are distinctly separate. The words אקרא וּבשׁם ה are repeated three times. In the first instance they are retrospective, but then swell into an always more full-toned vow of thanksgiving. The late period of its composition makes itself known not only in the strong Aramaic colouring of the form of the language, which adopts all kinds of embellishments, but also in many passages borrowed from the pre-exilic Psalms. The very opening, and still more so the progress, of the first strophe reminds one of Ps 18, and becomes an important hint for the exposition of the Psalm.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.116.1-Ps.116.4">Psa 116:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10103" type="x-p"/> Not only is כּי אהבתּי “I love (like, am well pleased) that,” like ἀγαπῶ ὅτι, Thucydides vi. 36, contrary to the usage of the language, but the thought, “I love that Jahve answereth me,” is also tame and flat, and inappropriate to the continuation in Psa 116:2. Since <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3-Ps.116.4">Psa 116:3-4</reference> have come from <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5-Ps.18.17">Psa 18:5-17</reference>, אהבתּי is to be understood according to ארחמך in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference>, so that it has the following יהוה as its object, not it is true grammatically, but logically. The poet is fond of this pregnant use of the verb without an expressed object, cf. אקרא in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.2">Psa 116:2</reference>, and האמנתּי in Psa 116:10. The <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> after ישׁמע is intended to guard against the blending of the final <hi type="italic">a‛</hi> with the initial <hi type="italic">'a</hi> of אדני (cf. Psa 56:1-13 :18; <reference osisRef="Ps.5.2">Psa 5:2</reference>, in Baer). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.116.1">Psa 116:1</reference></hi> the accentuation prevents the rendering <hi type="italic">vocem orationis meae</hi> (Vulgate, lxx) by means of <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>. The <hi type="italic">ı̂</hi> of קולי will therefore no more be the archaic connecting vowel (Ew. §211, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) than in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev 26:42</reference>; the poet has varied the genitival construction of <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">Psa 28:6</reference> to the permutative. The second כי, following close upon the first, makes the continuation of the confirmation retrospective. “In my days” is, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.39.8">Isa 39:8</reference>, Bar. 4:20, cf. בחיּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>, and frequently, equivalent to “so long as I live.” We even here hear the tone of Ps 18 (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference>), which is continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3-Ps.18.4">Psa 18:3-4</reference> as a freely borrowed passage. Instead of the “bands” (of Hades) there, the expression here is מצרי, <hi type="italic">angustiae</hi>, plural of meetsar, after the form מסב in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">Psa 118:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.3">Lam 1:3</reference> (Böttcher, <hi type="italic">De inferis</hi>, §423); the straitnesses of Hades are deadly perils which can scarcely be escaped. The futures אמצא and אקרא, by virtue of the connection, refer to the contemporaneous past. אנּה (viz., בלישׁן בקשׁה, i.e., in a suppliant sense) is written with <hi type="italic">He</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> here and in five other instances, as the Masora observes. It has its fixed <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> in the first syllable, in accordance with which it is to be pronounced <hi type="italic">ānna</hi> (like בּתּים, <hi type="italic">bāttim</hi>), and has an accented <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> not merely on account of the following יהוה = אדני (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Psa 3:8</reference>), but in every instance; for even where (the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> having been changed into a conjunctive) it is supplied with two different accents, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.50.17">Gen 50:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.31">Exo 32:31</reference>, the second indicates the tone-syllable.<note placement="foot">Kimchi, mistaking the vocation of the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, regards אנּה (אנּא) as <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>. But the Palestinian and the Babylonian systems of pointing coincide in this, that the beseeching אנא (אנה) is <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, and the interrogatory אנה <hi type="italic">Milel</hi> (with only two exceptions in our text, which is fixed according to the Palestinian Masora, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.139.7">Psa 139:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.28">Deu 1:28</reference>, where the following word begins with <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi>), and these modes of accenting accord with the origin of the two particles. Pinsker (<hi type="italic">Einleitung</hi>, S. xiii.) insinuates against the Palestinian system, that in the cases where אנא has two accents the pointing was not certain of the correct accentuation, only from a deficient knowledge of the bearings of the case.</note> <div eID="gen10103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10104" type="x-p"/> Instead now of repeating “and Jahve answered me,” the poet indulges in a laudatory confession of general truths which have been brought vividly to his mind by the answering of his prayer that he has experienced.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.116.5-Ps.116.9">Psa 116:5-9</reference> <div eID="gen10104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10105" type="x-p"/> With “gracious” and “compassionate” is here associated, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Psa 112:4</reference>, the term “righteous,” which comprehends within itself everything that Jahve asserts concerning Himself in Exo 34:6. from the words “and abundant in goodness and truth” onwards. His love is turned especially toward the simple (lxx τὰ νήπια, cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.11.25">Mat 11:25</reference>), who stand in need of His protection and give themselves over to it. פּתאים, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.9.6">Pro 9:6</reference>, is a mode of writing blended out of פּתאים and פּתיים. The poet also has experienced this love in a time of impotent need. דּלּותי is accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> here, and not as in <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">Psa 142:7</reference> on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. The accentuation is regulated by some phonetic or rhythmical law that has not yet been made clear (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference>).<note placement="foot">The national grammarians, so far as we are acquainted with them, furnish no explanation. De Balmis believes that these <hi type="italic">Milra</hi> forms דּלּותי, בּלּותי, and the like, must be regarded as infinitives, but at the same time confirms the difference of views existing on this point.</note> יהושׁיע is a resolved <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> form, the use of which became common in the later period of the language, but is not alien to the earlier period, especially in poetry (Ps 45:18, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Psa 81:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.47">1Sa 17:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Isa 52:5</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">Psa 116:7</reference> we hear the form of soliloquy which has become familiar to us from <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference>; Ps 103. שׁוּבי is <hi type="italic">Milra</hi> here, as also in two other instances. The plural מנוּחים signifies full, complete rest, as it is found only in God; and the suffix in the address to the soul is <hi type="italic">ajchi</hi> for <hi type="italic">ajich</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>-5. The perfect גּמל states that which is a matter of actual experience, and is corroborated in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.8">Psa 116:8</reference> in retrospective perfects. In <reference osisRef="Ps.116.8-Ps.116.9">Psa 116:8-9</reference> we hear Ps 56:14 again amplified; and if we add <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>, then we see as it were to the bottom of the origin of the poet’s thoughts. מן־דּמעה belongs still more decidedly than יהושׁיע to the resolved forms which multiply in the later period of the language. In <reference osisRef="Ps.116.9">Psa 116:9</reference> the poet declares the result of the divine deliverance. The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. אתהלּך denotes a free and contented going to and fro; and instead of “the land of the living,” <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>, the expression here is “the lands (ארצות), i.e., the broad land, of the living.” There he walks forth, with nothing to hinder his feet or limit his view, in the presence of Jahve, i.e., having his Deliverer from death ever before his eyes.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10-Ps.116.14">Psa 116:10-14</reference> <div eID="gen10105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10106" type="x-p"/> Since כּי אדבּר does not introduce anything that could become an object of belief, האמין is absolute here: to have faith, just as in <reference osisRef="Job.24.22">Job 24:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.24">Job 29:24</reference>, with לא it signifies “to be without faith, i.e., to despair.” But how does it now proceed? The lxx renders ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα, which the apostle makes use of in <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13">2Co 4:13</reference>, without our being therefore obliged with Luther to render<hi type="italic">: I believe, therefore I speak</hi>; כי does not signify διὸ. Nevertheless כי might according to the sense be used for לכן, if it had to be rendered with Hengstenberg: “I believed, therefore I spake,hy but I was very much plagued.” But this assertion does not suit this connection, and has, moreover, no support in the syntax. It might more readily be rendered: “I have believed that I should yet speak, i.e., that I should once more have a deliverance of God to celebrate;” but the connection of the parallel members, which is then only lax, is opposed to this. Hitzig’s attempted interpretation, “I trust, when (כּי as in <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer 12:1</reference>) I should speak: I am greatly afflicted,” i.e., “I have henceforth confidence, so that I shall not suffer myself to be drawn away into the expression of despondency,” does not commend itself, since <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference></hi> is a complaining, but not therefore as yet a desponding assertion of the reality. Assuming that האמנתּי and אמרתּי in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">Psa 116:11</reference></hi> stand on the same line in point of time, it seems that it must be interpreted <hi type="italic">I had faith, for I spake</hi> (was obliged to speak); but אדבר, separated from האמנתי by כי, is opposed to the colouring relating to the contemporaneous past. Thus <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference> will consequently contain the issue of that which has been hitherto experienced: <hi type="italic">I</hi> have gathered up faith and <hi type="italic">believe</hi> henceforth, <hi type="italic">when I speak</hi> (have to speak, must speak): <hi type="italic">I am deeply afflicted</hi> (ענה as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.67">Psa 119:67</reference>, cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">‛nâ</hi>, to be bowed down, more particularly in captivity, whence Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛nât</hi>, those who are bowed down). On the other hand, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">Psa 116:11</reference> is manifestly a retrospect. He believes now, for he is thoroughly weaned from putting trust in men: <hi type="italic">I said in my despair</hi> (taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>), the result of my deeply bowed down condition: <hi type="italic">All men are liars</hi> (πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ψεύστης, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Rom 3:4</reference>). Instead of המּות the poet, who is fond of such embellishments, chooses the pathetic form המּותה, and consequently, instead of the genitival construct state (מות), the construction with the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> of “belonging to.” It ought properly to be “soul” or “blood,” as in the primary passage Psa 72:14. But the observation of Grotius: <hi type="italic">quae pretiosa sunt, non facile largimur</hi>, applies also to the expression “death.” The death of His saints is no trifling matter with God; He does not lightly suffer it to come about; He does not suffer His own to be torn away from Him by death.<note placement="foot">The Apostolic Constitutions (vi. 30) commend the singing of these and other words of the Psalms at the funerals of those who have departed in the faith (cf. Augusti, <hi type="italic">Denkwürdigkeiten</hi>, ix. 563). In the reign of the Emperor Decius, Babylas Bishop of Antioch, full of blessed hope, met death singing these words.</note> <div eID="gen10107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10108" type="x-p"/> After this the poet goes on beseechingly: <hi type="italic">ānnáh Adonaj</hi>. The prayer itself is not contained in פּתּחתּ למוסרי - for he is already rescued, and the perfect as a precative is limited to such utterances spoken in the tone of an exclamation as we find in <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference> - but remains unexpressed; it lies wrapped up as it were in this heartfelt <hi type="italic">ānnáh</hi>: Oh remain still so gracious to me as Thou hast already proved Thyself to me. The poet rejoices in and is proud of the fact that he may call himself the servant of God. With אמתך he is mindful of his pious mother (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.86.16">Psa 86:16</reference>). The Hebrew does not form a feminine, עבדּה; Arab. <hi type="italic">amata</hi> signifies a maid, who is not, as such, also Arab. <hi type="italic">‛abdat</hi>, a slave. The dative of the object, למוסרי (from מוסרים for the more usual מוסרות), is used with פתחת instead of the accusative after the Aramaic manner, but it does also occur in the older Hebrew (e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa 53:11</reference>). The purpose of publicly giving thanks to the Gracious One is now more full-toned here at the close. Since such emphasis is laid on the Temple and the congregation, what is meant is literal thank-offerings in payment of vows. In בּתוככי (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.135.9">Psa 135:9</reference>) we have in the suffix the ancient and Aramaic <hi type="italic">i</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">Psa 116:7</reference>) for the third time. With אנּה the poet clings to Jahve, with נגדּה־נּא to the congregation, and with בּתוככי to the holy city. The one thought that fills his whole soul, and in which the song which breathes forth his soul dies away, is <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi>.  <chapter eID="Ps.116"/> <div eID="gen10108" type="x-p"/>
